Research task. Produce a decision-grade briefing, not a tutorial. You have WebSearch/WebFetch.

CONTEXT: Joe self-hosts a small personal PaaS on an M1 Pro Mac (16GB). Each "app" gets an isolated environment he ssh's into from his phone, containing his code and an LLM coding harness (pi, Claude Code). Today envs are Docker/OrbStack containers built from a shared image. He rejects the current model because: (1) plain `apk add` doesn't survive image rebuilds, so I added a custom `envpkg` wrapper that records packages and replays them — he objects that "no other harness knows how to use that" (an LLM agent in the env will just type `apt install`), and believes a wrapper shouldn't be necessary at all; (2) he wants "an effective VPS on my own machine": he handles his own repos, installs whatever he wants, and the platform never wipes or resets anything it didn't create itself.

HIS QUESTION: "Would a system like nix on those hosts make this easier to manage?"

ANSWER THESE, with citations, and flag uncertainty honestly:
1. What specifically would Nix (or NixOS) solve here that a plain persistent-rootfs VM/system-container would not? Be concrete about: reproducible baseline, in-place upgrades that don't destroy user state, rollback, and per-env declarative config.

The correct design turned out to be strictly simpler: the daemon's only network client was the dashboard all along, so one bridge-bound listener with a peer allowlist suffices and the second listener is unnecessary"; action "before designing any change to how component A reaches component B, read A's source and confirm the coupling exists — grep for the port, the URL, the client library. The existence of a server, a credential, or a config entry naming an endpoint is not evidence that a given caller uses it; something else may be the only client. A phantom coupling makes the design strictly more complex than reality requires and can destroy an independence property that was never in danger, and the failure mode is invisible in review because the prose describing the swap reads perfectly plausibly. Corollary: when a design claims to 'preserve' a property by changing a mechanism, check whether the property currently holds BECAUSE that mechanism is absent"

Handoff from learn (opening capture, single note — a confirmed self-discovered reversal). kind=feedback; slug tailnet-acls-do-not-govern-traffic-that-never-enters-wireguard; source "session 2026-08-07, context: phone-llm — I designed and shipped a tailnet ACL as the platform's 'one app-proof enforcement point' for app-to-app isolation, then a check found a logged-out machine reaching another app's TAILNET IP and getting a root shell over Tailscale SSH"; situation "relying on a tailnet/overlay-network ACL (Tailscale, Nebula, ZeroTier) to isolate peers that ALSO share an underlay — a bridge, a LAN segment, a hypervisor's virtual switch, or a shared kernel's routing table"; behavior "treated a tailnet ACL as the enforcement point for machine-to-machine isolation, reasoning that all three app nodes carried tag:apps and the policy was default-deny, and wrote into the design that this was 'the one chokepoint no app can override'. Verified the rule worked by testing between two machines that were both joined to the tailnet, and generalised from that"; impact "the ACL governs WireGuard-encapsulated traffic only. A machine on the same underlay can address a peer's 100.x tailnet IP directly — `ip route get` showed it going via the OrbStack bridge gateway on eth0, not via any tailscale0 interface — so the policy never sees the packets. Measured: a machine LOGGED OUT of the tailnet, with no tailscale0 at all, resolved a peer's MagicDNS name, fetched its app on :8080 (200), and obtained a root shell via Tailscale SSH, while the policy explicitly refused app-to-app SSH for joined peers. The design doc, the README enforcement table, and the change's spec delta all asserted a guarantee the substrate could not provide"; action "before crediting an overlay ACL with isolating two hosts, establish whether those hosts can reach each other WITHOUT the overlay — and test from a host that is NOT joined to it, since a joined host's traffic is encapsulated and will honour the policy no matter what the underlay permits. Two joined peers testing clean proves the policy works for peers, not that the boundary holds. Where an underlay exists, the ACL protects the overlay plane against overlay members; the only thing that stops an underlay neighbour is not listening on a reachable address. Corollary: an overlay IP is not a private address — it is routable by anything that has a route to it"

  --situation "restarting the OrbStack engine, or debugging why host.orb.internal stopped resolving inside an OrbStack machine that also runs tailscale" \

  --object "measured 2026-08-03: after 'orbctl stop', /etc/resolv.conf in every env contained ONLY tailscale MagicDNS (nameserver 100.100.100.100 + fd7a:115c:a1e0::53) with no fallback, so host.orb.internal AND ordinary public DNS both failed inside the envs. systemd-resolved was inactive, so tailscale took the file over in direct mode and dropped OrbStack's resolver. SYMPTOMS ARE MISLEADING: public app URLs stayed 200/302 throughout because ingress is INBOUND over the tailnet and needs no DNS inside the env; what broke was anything the env initiates — the dashboard's proxy to apphostd returned 502, and pi could not reach the model service. curl exits 6 (couldn't resolve), not 7 (refused), which distinguishes this from a service being down. (2) TEST THE CAPABILITY, NOT THE ARTIFACT — assert on the thing you actually care about being impossible.   --object "measured 2026-08-03: the todo app's /app/run does 'make build' for a Go server.   --source "session 2026-08-03, context: phone-llm — a Gate A reviewer caught that my remediation plan closed the path by which a public app had read the control token, but scheduled rotating that token two groups later" \
  --situation "remediating a credential exposure — planning the order of a fix after a secret was readable, or reachable, by something that should not have had it" \
  --behavior "sequenced the plan around the vulnerability rather than the compromise: group 1 closed the filesystem path that leaked the token and was labelled 'the whole point', with rotation demoted to group 3 and everything after group 1 called 'consolidation'" \
  --impact "the specific credential had been demonstrated in the attacker position minutes earlier — read by a public app and used to drive the control plane. Under that ordering it stayed valid through two more groups, so the plan would have reported the exposure closed while the working stolen credential was still accepted. A reviewer caught it; the framing had made it look finished" \
  --action "treat every exposed credential as two separate remediations that both belong in the first wave: close the PATH, and invalidate the VALUE that travelled it. Closing the path only stops future reads. If a secret was readable by something untrusted, assume it was read — rotation is not hardening to schedule later, it is half the fix. Enumerate every consumer before rotating, because a secret is usually pasted in more places than the file it came from: here the daemon re-read its file per request but the client cached it at process start from a hand-placed systemd drop-in, so rotating the source alone would have 401'd the client" 2>&1 | tail -2

  --source "session 2026-08-04, context: phone-llm — I shipped a deny-list as an interim fix inside change 'apps-serve-a-site-not-a-repo', whose own design named site-root separation as the durable follow-up.   --situation "about to open a new change, issue, or ticket for work that an existing open one already named as its own follow-up, interim step, or deferred half" \
  --behavior "opened a second change for the durable fix that the first change's design had explicitly deferred to 'later', even though the first was still open and unarchived — then had to invent an ordering dependency ('A must archive before B's delta resolves') to make the two coexist, because both modified the same requirement" \
  --impact "split one arc of intent across two records, so neither told the whole story: the first looked like it shipped a weak fix and stopped, the second looked like it appeared from nowhere. It also manufactured a real coupling — the second change could not be applied or synced until the first archived — which is cost paid for a boundary that should not have existed. The user had to point out that we were evolving a change, not starting one" \
  --action "when an open change's own artifacts name a follow-up, that follow-up is a continuation of it: evolve the change — extend its proposal, add decisions to its design, strengthen the same delta, append task groups — rather than opening a sibling. Changes are units of intent, and shipping an interim step does not close the intent. THE TELL: if you find yourself writing 'change A must archive before change B', or two changes MODIFY the same requirement, they are one change. Open a genuinely new change only when the intent is new — not when the momentum of having already committed the first one makes editing it feel like backtracking" 2>&1 | tail -2

engram learn feedback --slug tailnet-acls-do-not-govern-traffic-that-never-enters-wireguard --position top \
  --source "session 2026-08-07, context: phone-llm — I designed and shipped a tailnet ACL as the platform's 'one app-proof enforcement point' for app-to-app isolation, then a check found a logged-out machine reaching another app's TAILNET IP and getting a root shell over Tailscale SSH" \
  --situation "relying on a tailnet/overlay-network ACL (Tailscale, Nebula, ZeroTier) to isolate peers that ALSO share an underlay — a bridge, a LAN segment, a hypervisor's virtual switch, or a shared kernel's routing table" \
  --behavior "treated a tailnet ACL as the enforcement point for machine-to-machine isolation, reasoning that all three app nodes carried tag:apps and the policy was default-deny, and wrote into the design that this was 'the one chokepoint no app can override'. Verified the rule worked by testing between two machines that were both joined to the tailnet, and generalised from that" \
  --impact "the ACL governs WireGuard-encapsulated traffic only. A machine on the same underlay can address a peer's 100.x tailnet IP directly — 'ip route get' showed it going via the OrbStack bridge gateway on eth0, not via any tailscale0 interface — so the policy never sees the packets. Measured: a machine LOGGED OUT of the tailnet, with no tailscale0 at all, resolved a peer's MagicDNS name, fetched its app on :8080 (200), and obtained a root shell via Tailscale SSH, while the policy explicitly refused app-to-app SSH for joined peers. The design doc, the README enforcement table, and the change's spec delta all asserted a guarantee the substrate could not provide" \
  --action "before crediting an overlay ACL with isolating two hosts, establish whether those hosts can reach each other WITHOUT the overlay — and test from a host that is NOT joined to it, since a joined host's traffic is encapsulated and will honour the policy no matter what the underlay permits. Two joined peers testing clean proves the policy works for peers, not that the boundary holds. Where an underlay exists, the ACL protects the overlay plane against overlay members; the only thing that stops an underlay neighbour is not listening on a reachable address. Corollary: an overlay IP is not a private address — it is routable by anything that has a route to it" 2>&1 | tail -3

learn_calls.skill_args: Mid-cycle fast path, single confirmed correction. Context: implementing phone-llm's integrations-run-inside-the-app. A live verification test (task 4.4) caught a real defect: app_services() — a READ path — correctly classified a substituted service on a registered port as "IDENTITY CHANGED" and rendered the per-signal diff, but left the ingress route up and the unix socket serving the substitute. The fail-closed enforcement lived only in verify_integration(), which nothing on the read path called. So the platform detected the confused-deputy state, displayed a warning about it, and went on serving an unknown service under a registered name and inside its Access gate. Confirmed by live measurement, then reproduced as a RED unit test, then fixed by extracting _enforce_identity() and calling it from BOTH app_services() and verify_integration(). Lesson: when a classification identifies a security-relevant state, the code path that OBSERVES it must also ACT on it — a read that only reports the state has not failed closed, it has narrated. Splitting detection (a read) from enforcement (a separate function) leaves a window where the platform knows and serves anyway. Corollary confirmed in the same session: unit tests + a 5-mutation check all passed while this defect was live; only the end-to-end substitution test on real infrastructure found it.

HANDOFF from learn (mid-cycle, self-discovered reversal).

When reviewing such a design, ask of each observer "does it act, or only report?"

## Verification Report — A1 bypass-fixture plan (revised)

Method: read the plan and both live source files in full; additionally wrote isolated dash (strict POSIX sh) reproductions of the exact trap snippet and ran them under real signals, and simulated the awk single-source-of-truth extraction against the real `appctl_lib.py` content, rather than reasoning about shell semantics from memory.

### 1. POSIX sh trap mechanism (§3) — holds structurally, but has one real gap

Confirmed via `dash -n` (syntax) and two live runs under `dash` with a stubbed `orb`:

- **Happy path** (no interrupt): `bypass_active` as a plain (non-`local`) variable is correctly shared between the top-level block and `bypass_cleanup()` — no subshell separates them, and it's assigned (`bypass_active=0`) before the trap is armed, so `set -u` never sees it unbound. The manual `bypass_cleanup` call followed by `trap - EXIT INT TERM` disarms cleanly: cleanup ran exactly once, no double-fire at script exit. This part of the plan holds.

- **Interrupt path** — this is the real finding. I sent `kill -TERM` to a running instance of the exact snippet mid-"probe":
```
sleeping...
cleanup ran
AFTER SLEEP - script resumed instead of terminating
exit code: 0
```
`trap bypass_cleanup EXIT INT TERM` **restores state correctly** (tailscaled restarted, fixture stopped — the safety property the plan exists to guarantee does hold). But because `bypass_cleanup` never calls `exit`, POSIX/dash trap semantics mean the shell **does not terminate on SIGINT/SIGTERM** — it resumes execution right after the interrupted command and runs the rest of `check-isolation` to completion as if nothing happened. A Ctrl-C or `kill` during the bypass section will not actually stop the check; it'll look like the interrupt did nothing.

This is a real, verified gap, not the same one already fixed (state restoration works fine). The plan's own §6 test ("confirm the trap actually restores tailscaled and stops the fixture") won't catch it, because it only checks restoration, not termination.

**What better looks like:** separate the EXIT trap from the INT/TERM traps, and have the latter explicitly exit after cleanup:
```sh
trap bypass_cleanup EXIT
trap 'bypass_cleanup; trap - INT TERM; kill -$$ ...; exit 130' INT TERM
```
(or the simpler idiom: `trap 'bypass_cleanup; exit 130' INT TERM` plus `trap bypass_cleanup EXIT`, being mindful that `exit` inside the INT/TERM handler re-fires the EXIT trap — harmless here since `bypass_cleanup` is idempotent on `bypass_active=0`, but worth a comment so it isn't "fixed" into an infinite loop later).

### 2. `getent hosts` inside golden — holds (narrow question), with a bigger caveat worth surfacing

`bin/build-golden`'s package list (`python3 python3-venv git curl ca-certificates build-essential nodejs npm less jq fish`) never installs `getent` explicitly — correctly so: `getent` ships in `libc-bin`, `Priority: required`/`Essential: yes` on every Debian/Ubuntu base, including OrbStack's `ubuntu` cloud image. No network install needed; the plan's assumption of availability is safe.

Bigger unaddressed risk, surfaced because it bears directly on whether §6's "expected right now" claims will actually hold: MagicDNS resolution for `*.$TAILNET` names is served by `tailscaled` itself (typically via a stub resolver wired to 100.100.100.100). The DNS check runs *after* `systemctl stop tailscaled`. It's plausible `getent hosts other.$TAILNET` will fail to resolve for **every** neighbour once tailscaled is down — not because of any ACL property, but because the resolver process is gone — which would make the DNS-first `fail`/`continue` fire on every iteration and never actually exercise `denied()`/`ssh_blocked()` for the HTTP/SSH plane at all. To the plan's credit, §6 already treats "confirm the DNS check passes for every real app" as something to verify live rather than assume, and fails loudly rather than silently if it doesn't — so this isn't an unhandled gap in process, but it's underplayed as a risk given it could invalidate the documented "expected: HTTP-plane PASS" result. Worth watching closely on the first real run.

### 3. Single source of truth (`BYPASS` constant) — holds, verified by simulation

Line 34 of the real `appctl_lib.py` is exactly `GOLDEN = "apphost-golden"`. I inserted `BYPASS = "apphost-bypass"` immediately after it (as the plan specifies) and ran the plan's exact awk command against the resulting file:
```
GOLDEN=[apphost-golden]
BYPASS=[apphost-bypass]
```
Identical extraction mechanism, confirmed working. No existing `BYPASS` symbol anywhere in the current file that could collide with the `^BYPASS = ` anchor.

### 4. `running=`/`stopped=` exclusion (lines 61–62, 76–77) — holds, correct minimal fix

Read verbatim:
```sh
running=$(orb list 2>/dev/null | awk '$1!="NAME" && $2=="running" {print $1}' \
          | grep -v '^docker$' | grep -v "^$GOLDEN$")
...
machines=${*:-$running}
neighbours=$running
...
stopped=$(orb list 2>/dev/null | awk '$1!="NAME" && $2!="running" {print $1}' \
          | grep -v '^docker$' | grep -v "^$GOLDEN$")
```
Appending `| grep -v "^$BYPASS$"` to both mirrors the existing GOLDEN-exclusion exactly (same shape, third pipe stage). No unintended interaction with line 68's arg-narrowing: with no args, `machines` (and `neighbours`) now skip BYPASS from the default set, exactly as GOLDEN already is skipped. Explicit-argument invocation (`check-isolation apphost-bypass`) still bypasses the `$running`-based exclusion entirely — but that's pre-existing behavior identical to how `check-isolation apphost-golden` already works today, not a new side effect introduced by this change.

### 5. design.md wording (§5) — holds

Read both files in full. `ingress-identity-cannot-be-borrowed/design.md` decision 8 (lines 333–334) already contains the precedent format: `**Resolved 2026-08-08:** relax the contract.` — the plan's proposed sentence for the sibling file, `**Resolved 2026-08-08: dedicated machine kept stopped, started only for the check** (per Joe).`, matches this exact shape: states the decision plainly, no "X rather than Y" comparison, no invented "because" beyond what's attributed to Joe. Confirmed the two currently-open cross-references the plan says to update both still say "owned by `only-owner-devices-open-a-shell` decision 4" and treat it as open (decision 8's resolution paragraph, lines 336–338, and the Open Questions bullet, lines 342–344) — matches the plan's described starting state, and the proposed pointer-only fix matches the same authoritative-source-plus-pointer pattern already used bidirectionally between these two files.

Minor caveat: I could not find any in-repo record of the "Cycle 2" precedent the revision note cites twice (grepped both change directories, the whole repo, and git log for "Cycle 2" — no hits). Likely an out-of-band conversation with Joe not captured in a tracked file; I can only confirm the proposed wording's *shape* matches the in-repo precedent I could find, not the origin of the rule itself.

### Bottom line

4 of 5 points hold as designed. Point 1 has a genuine, empirically-confirmed gap: the trap restores fleet state correctly but does not stop the script on an actual interrupt, which the plan's own live-fleet test (§6) is not positioned to catch since it only checks restoration. Recommend fixing the INT/TERM trap to explicitly `exit` after cleanup before running §6's live verification, so the interrupt test proves both properties (state restored *and* the run actually stops) rather than just one.

(1) PROPOSAL INTENT (proposal.md)

Why (verbatim, full): "Kind-4 confirmed-approaches (\"what worked, do it again\") currently live awkwardly inside `feedback` notes' action/behavior/impact fields rather than as reusable, retrievable, task-type-keyed procedures. SPL research shows procedural-strategy injection lifts weak models materially (OptiLLMBench +4%, AIME24 +7%, Arena-Hard +8.6%). Joe decided (2026-08-08) this warrants a new first-class content kind rather than a tag convention on `feedback`. Related: #718 (efficacy tracking), #685 (task-kind glance cue), purview check #293."

What Changes:
- New `procedure` note kind (frontmatter `type: procedure`), distinct from `fact | feedback | qa`, for task-type-keyed "how to approach X" strategy notes.
- Wire through all four touch points, mirroring how `qa` was added end-to-end: `engram learn` (capture path accepts/produces procedure notes); `write-memory` (composes/executes the vault-write command); `recall`/`query` (retrieval surfaces procedure notes; ranking vs situation-similarity decided during implementation per design.md).
- "Introduce a task-type taxonomy field, derived free-form from the captured procedure's own subject rather than a fixed enum (SPL's 16-type set is benchmark-tuned, not engram-native). Anchor skill docs with 2-3 concrete engram examples (e.g. \"running eval harnesses\", \"releasing Go modules\", \"recall-moment discovery\")."
- Decide and document (in design.md, carried into the PR/commit) the surfacing mechanism: new recall Step-1 phrase, pre-filter, or separate retrieval path.
- "Validation gate before shipping (documented in design.md, executed as tasks): (1) vault supply check — how much existing kind-4 content is already procedure-shaped, (2) A/B recall test on a recurring task class, (3) cross-check against SPL's own eval methodology."

Capabilities: NEW `learn-procedure-capture` ("`engram learn` capture path + frontmatter schema for the new `procedure` note kind, and the write-memory compose/execute wiring for it — mirrors `learn-qa-capture`'s role for `qa`") and NEW `recall-procedure-surfacing` ("how `procedure` notes are retrieved and ranked in `recall`/`query` against situation-similarity, including the task-type taxonomy and its surfacing mechanism (Step-1 phrase / pre-filter / separate path)"). MODIFIED: "(none — no existing spec's requirements change; `qa`, `fact`, `feedback` handling is untouched)".

Impact: `internal/cli` (frontmatter schema + learn capture wiring); `agent-instructions/skills/write-memory/SKILL.md` (compose/execute support, per `superpowers:writing-skills` TDD); `agent-instructions/skills/learn/SKILL.md` (capture guidance + task-type taxonomy examples); `agent-instructions/skills/recall/SKILL.md` (retrieval/ranking guidance); `internal/cli` query path ("new kind participates in `candidate_l2s` (or an equivalent decided retrieval path)"); vault content ("a supply-check mining pass over existing kind-4 feedback notes to validate real demand before shipping").

Issues referenced: #718 (efficacy tracking — explicitly deferred), #685 (task-kind glance cue), #293 (purview check).

====================================================================
(2) DESIGN.MD — ALL SECTIONS

Context: Four content kinds exist today: `fact | feedback | qa` (qa splits into `qa-question`/`qa-answer` at frontmatter `type` level). Each kind wired through the same four touch points: `engram learn` (capture), `write-memory` (compose/execute the write), `recall`/`query` (retrieval), skill docs. `qa` is the most recent addition (`openspec/specs/learn-qa-capture/spec.md`) and closest structural analog, "including `isQueryExcludedKind` (`internal/cli/qa.go`) for kinds that need partial retrieval exclusion." Normative: "`procedure` notes have no reason for asymmetric exclusion — unlike a `qa-question` (which exists only to be pointed at), a `procedure` note's content (a task-type + strategy) is itself the retrieval target. It SHALL compete in the main matched set like `qa-answer` and `fact`/`feedback` notes."

Goals: (a) "Add `type: procedure` as a fully wired first-class kind, symmetric with `fact`/`feedback` (not asymmetric like `qa`)."; (b) "Free-form task-type taxonomy, seeded by 2-3 engram-native examples, not a fixed enum."; (c) "A documented, evidence-gated decision on the surfacing mechanism (Step-1 phrase vs pre-filter vs separate retrieval path)."; (d) "A pre-ship validation gate: vault supply check, A/B recall test, SPL methodology cross-check."

Non-Goals: (a) "Per-note efficacy/outcome tracking (success_count/total_attempts, SPL-style ranking formula) — that's #718, explicitly deferred."; (b) "A fixed 16-type taxonomy — SPL's set is benchmark-tuned, not adopted."; (c) "Retrofitting existing `feedback` notes into `procedure` notes — this change adds the new kind; migrating the vault's existing kind-4 content is a follow-up informed by the supply-check task, not part of this change's acceptance criteria."

Decisions (4):
- Decision 1 — Frontmatter shape: "`type: procedure`, plus a `task_type: <free-form-slug>` field (e.g. `running-eval-harnesses`, `releasing-go-modules`, `recall-moment-discovery`), derived from the captured procedure's own subject at capture time — not selected from a hardcoded enum." Rationale: SPL's fixed taxonomy is benchmark-tuned; engram's task surface doesn't map onto it; free-form lets the taxonomy emerge from actual usage (validated by supply-check) instead of being guessed up front.
- Decision 2 — Retrieval treatment, compete don't exclude: "`procedure` is NOT added to `isQueryExcludedKind`. It participates in `candidate_l2s` like `fact`/`feedback`/`qa-answer`." Rationale: the whole content (task-type-keyed strategy) is the thing worth retrieving; no paired "question" half to hide.
- Decision 3 — Surfacing mechanism: "pre-filter on `task_type`, not a new Step-1 phrase". "When `query`/`recall` is invoked with the calling agent's inferred task type, `procedure` notes whose `task_type` matches (exact or embedding-similar) are boosted/pre-filtered ahead of pure situation-similarity ranking, mirroring the matched-note floor pattern already shipped for note-vs-chunk ranking (`recall-matched-note-floor` spec, `capWithNoteFloor`)." Rationale: a new Step-1 phrase would touch Step-1 sequencing depended on by other kinds (higher blast radius); a pre-filter/floor is additive and isolated to procedure notes. "This choice and its rationale MUST be restated in the shipping commit/PR per the proposal's acceptance criteria."
- Decision 4 — Validation gate sequenced before recall-ranking task: supply-check and A/B test "both need the capture path to exist first (to know what a real `procedure` note looks like) but must complete BEFORE the pre-filter ranking logic (`Decision 3`) ships, since the A/B test's outcome could revise the surfacing mechanism decision. Tasks.md sequences: capture/schema → supply check → A/B test → (confirm or revise Decision 3) → ranking implementation → skill docs."

Risks / Trade-offs (3):
- Free-form `task_type` fragments into near-duplicate slugs (`run-eval-harness` vs `running-eval-harnesses`) hurting pre-filter match rate → mitigation: "pre-filter matches by embedding similarity on `task_type`, not exact string equality"; supply-check surfaces whether normalization guidance is needed in learn skill docs.
- Pre-filter boost over-fires and buries good situation-similarity matches for non-matching task types → mitigation: "the A/B recall test (acceptance criterion 3) is a hard gate before the ranking logic ships, not an optional nice-to-have; if it shows no lift or regression, Decision 3 is revisited before implementation continues."
- Validation gate findings could invalidate the whole change post-capture-implementation → mitigation: intentional; "tasks.md must not implement the ranking/surfacing step until the gate passes, and if the gate fails, tasks.md's remaining ranking/doc tasks become the record of what to reconsider rather than being silently skipped."

Migration Plan: "No data migration — this is purely additive (new kind, no changes to existing `fact`/`feedback`/`qa` handling). Rollback is a revert of the four touch-point changes; no vault content needs to be un-migrated since existing kind-4 content stays in `feedback` notes unless a future, separate change proposes migrating it."

Open Questions (2): exact `task_type` embedding-similarity threshold for the pre-filter ("left to implementation/eval, not fixed here"); whether the supply-check finds enough existing procedure-shaped content to bootstrap a meaningful A/B test population or synthetic/seeded procedure notes are needed first ("resolved by the supply-check task itself").

All research complete. Here is the compact factual summary.

## 1. Prompt-cache reuse for hybrid models (issue #980) — FIXED in v0.31.x for the normal chat pattern

- Issue #980 ("Prefix cache reuse is broken for all hybrid-architecture models") was opened 2026-03-11 and **closed as completed 2026-04-14** by maintainer angeloskath: "Closing because this issue is now quite outdated. The latest release supports caching of the system prompt and the user messages resulting in minimal prompt reprocessing (it can still be a lot of tokens but it can't be helped as the past reasoning is dropped from the conversation)." — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/issues/980 (state_reason "completed" confirmed via GitHub API)
- The community fix PRs stayed unmerged (#999 still open, #1006 closed unmerged), but the maintainer's **PR #1019 "Refactor LRUPromptCache" merged 2026-03-26** and shipped in v0.31.2, whose release notes list "Caching system prompt and user messages for non-trimmable caches." — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/pull/1019 , https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/releases/tag/v0.31.2
- Verified directly in v0.31.3 source: `LRUPromptCache.fetch_nearest_cache` (mlx_lm/models/cache.py, ~L1674) has three paths — exact-match deepcopy, **shorter-prefix deepcopy (no trimming needed — this is what works for hybrids)**, and a longer-entry trim path gated on `can_trim_prompt_cache`, which returns False for `ArraysCache` (GatedDeltaNet recurrent state). The server also snapshots caches at segment boundaries (end of system prompt, end of user messages, pre-thinking tail) via `insert_cache(cache_type="system"/"user")` during prefill (server.py ~L868-880), and Qwen3.5/3.6-style hybrids qualify because `ArraysCache` implements `merge`. — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/v0.31.3/mlx_lm/models/cache.py , https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/v0.31.3/mlx_lm/server.py
- **Net for Bonsai/Qwen3.6 on v0.31.3:** sequential multi-turn chat does NOT fully re-prefill — each turn reuses the cached prefix and processes only new tokens. Residual re-prefill: (a) the previous assistant turn is reprocessed because Qwen-family chat templates strip thinking traces from history (maintainer comment in #980); (b) any rewind/divergence before a checkpoint can't be trimmed for SSM state, falling back to the nearest shorter checkpoint or full recompute (divergent-suffix concurrent-agent pattern, per #980 discussion).
- Caveat: PrismML's own docs still claim "MLX has no cross-request prompt cache, so multi-turn conversations reprocess the full history" — contradicted by the v0.31.x server source above; likely outdated or referring to `mlx_lm.generate`. — https://docs.prismml.com/run/mlx . An April 2026 report of 0% reuse with Qwen3-Next was via LM Studio's mlx-engine, a different serving stack. — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/issues/980

## 2. Memory-safety options in mlx_lm.server v0.31.3

Verified from the v0.31.3 server.py argparse block (https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/v0.31.3/mlx_lm/server.py):
- **No KV-cache quantization flags** — no `--kv-bits`, `--kv-group-size`, `--quantized-kv-start`, no `--max-kv-size`. Issue #1308 (opened 2026-05-24, **still open**) requests exactly these for the server. — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/issues/1308
- **No max-context/prompt-length limit and no memory ceiling flag.** The only guards: `--prompt-cache-size` (default 10 cached sequences), `--prompt-cache-bytes` (byte cap on the cache LRU), `--prefill-step-size` (default 2048), `--max-tokens` (default 512 per request). The server sets `mx.set_wired_limit(max_recommended_working_set_size)` automatically (L1889).
- **Default port 8080**, host 127.0.0.1.
- Related open memory issue: Metal OOM during long-context prefill on Qwen3.5/3.6 hybrid MoE (transient prefill workspace, not KV size), issue #1480, open, 2026-07-06. — https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/issues/1480

## 3. Bonsai on stock mlx-lm

- **The model card recommends stock mlx-lm**: `pip install --upgrade mlx-lm`, `mlx_lm.chat --model "prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-27B-mlx-2bit"`, `mlx_lm.server --model ...`. — https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-27B-mlx-2bit
- PrismML docs: **ternary (2-bit) works with stock MLX; only 1-bit needs the PrismML fork** (pending upstream mlx PR #3161). Recommended sampling `--temp 0.5 --top-p 0.85`. — https://docs.prismml.com/run/mlx
- The MLX pack's config.json is `model_type: "qwen3_5"` with **standard MLX affine quantization `{bits: 2, group_size: 128}`** — so stock mlx-lm runs it through its generic 2-bit quantized-matmul path, and v0.31.3 has native `qwen3_5` support (models/qwen3_5.py: GatedDeltaNet + ArraysCache/KVCache, handles text_config). — https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-27B-mlx-2bit/resolve/main/config.json , https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/v0.31.3/mlx_lm/models/qwen3_5.py
- **Stock mlx-lm has no dedicated Bonsai low-bit decode kernels.** Dedicated kernels exist in oMLX 0.5.2 ("dedicated decode kernels for the bonsai models") and PrismML's forks; the reference datapoint is 10-12 tok/s without them vs ~25 tok/s expected on an M4 Pro (PrismML staff, HF discussion #2). CONTEXT: appingressd is a new launchd daemon that will sit on the ingress path for a self-hosted app platform. cloudflared's origin becomes `unix:~/.config/apphost/ingress/<app>.sock`; the daemon pipes each connection to the app's own loopback via `orb -m <app> -u root nc 127.0.0.1 8080`. If it dies, every app is down. A machine-state guard was just added because `orb exec` auto-starts a stopped machine, which would let an unauthenticated request boot an environment.

Is there a path where a connection hangs forever, or a zombie/FD leak accumulates?
2. **Does the guard actually sit at the right layer?** It is checked per connection inside `_handle`. Is that the right seam, or should it be elsewhere? Is `machine_running()`'s bare `except Exception: return False` hiding real errors that should be logged?
3. **SRP/DRY.** Is `Forwarder` doing too much (socket lifecycle + process management + byte pumping)? Is there duplication with `apphostd`/`votek-ensured` that should be shared? Is `UNAVAILABLE` as a hardcoded byte-string with a hand-counted Content-Length a latent bug (count the bytes yourself and verify it matches).

Are there obvious cases it misses that would bite in production — a slow backend, a large response, a client that disconnects mid-response, two concurrent connections to the same socket?

ARTIFACT: `bin/appingressd` and `bin/test_appingressd.py` in the WORKING TREE (uncommitted), specifically the `_handle` rewrite. Compare against `git show HEAD:bin/appingressd`.

WHAT CHANGED AND WHY. The handler was two blocking threads (one pumping client->backend, one backend->client). Measured against the live fleet: 20 requests left 21 `nc` processes in the machine and 21 `orb` children on the host, climbing — one process and one thread leaked per request. Cause: the backend is `nc` talking to an HTTP server holding a keep-alive connection open, so it never exits; the reader parked in `read1()` forever and the teardown in `finally` never ran. `/bin/cat` could not reproduce it (cat exits on EOF), so the guard test passed throughout. Replaced with ONE `select` loop that terminates the backend rather than waiting on it. Re-measured: zero leaked processes after the idle window.

ATTACK SPECIFICALLY:
1. **Is the select loop correct?** Trace it. Can it spin hot? Can it drop buffered data when one side closes? Does `client_done` handling lose data the backend still had to send? What happens if `proc.stdin.write` raises (backend already dead)? Is the `except (OSError, ValueError)` too broad — does it hide a real bug?
2. **The two timeouts** (`IDLE_TIMEOUT=120` pre-request, `RESPONSE_IDLE=30` post-request) are both now constructor params. Is that YAGNI-violating configurability, or earned testability? Is 30s defensible given `apphostd` serializes requests (issue #8)? Is there a case where a legitimate slow response gets cut?
3. **Reaping**: `proc.terminate()` then `wait(timeout=5)` then `kill()`. For `orb -m X -u root nc ...`, does SIGTERM to the *orb* process actually kill the `nc` INSIDE the machine, or could it orphan the in-machine process? This matters — the leak was in-machine `nc` processes. Reason about it; the author measured zero afterwards, but check whether that proves the mechanism or just correlates.
4. **The test**: it now ends with `os._exit()` instead of `sys.exit()`, and every Forwarder takes short timeouts. Is `os._exit` masking something? Are the short timeouts making the test prove less than production behavior?
5. **SRP/DRY**: is `_handle` now doing too much (guard, spawn, pump, teardown)? Would this read as coherent to someone who did not watch it evolve?
6. Anything left over from the two-thread design that is now dead or misleading — imports, comments, docstring claims.

OUTPUT: numbered findings, file:line + why it fails design-fit + concretely what better looks like. Do not fix anything.

learn_calls.skill_args: Crystallize confirmed mechanism for phone-llm#9: OrbStack relays a machine's 100.64/10 (tailnet) traffic onto the Mac's tailscale, SNAT'd to the Mac's own tailnet identity which is tag:ingress. PROVEN by apphostd log showing "refused 100.70.216.20" (the Mac's tailnet IP, tag:ingress) for a bypass connection whose grant is held by dash. So every OrbStack machine — even one logged out of tailscale — reaches every app's :8080 and :22 by routing to a tailnet IP via the OrbStack gateway (192.168.139.1 dev eth0), because the ACL must allow tag:ingress -> tag:apps and the relay borrows tag:ingress. A JOINED machine is only incidentally blocked because tailscale's own client nft rule (ts-input: drop saddr 100.64.0.0/10 iifname != tailscale0) drops the relayed reply; root in the machine can remove that or `tailscale logout`, so the bypass is available to every env always. Host pf cannot filter it (net.inet.ip.forwarding=0 changed nothing => userspace re-origination; egress is indistinguishable from cloudflared, both leave utun9 as 100.70.216.20 -> app). OrbStack 2.2.1 has no config to suppress routing 100.64/10 from machines (isolate_network is broken/inverted). The control plane survived only because apphostd has a second per-grant-address check the apps lack. This is the mechanism issue 9 listed as "not yet established."

kind=fact
slug=orbstack-relays-machine-tailnet-traffic-as-tag-ingress-identity
source=session 2026-08-07, context: debugging phone-llm#9 — confirmed the tailnet-bypass mechanism the issue listed as "not yet established", by reading apphostd's refused-peer log
situation=debugging or hardening why an OrbStack machine can reach a tailnet address (another app, the host) it should not, on the phone-llm platform; or designing the fix for only-ingress-reaches-an-app / issue #9
subject=OrbStack (2.2.1) relaying a Linux machine's 100.64.0.0/10 (tailnet) traffic through its gateway (192.168.139.1 dev eth0) onto the macOS host's tailscale
predicate=re-originates the connection SNAT'd to the Mac's own tailnet identity, which carries tag:ingress — so the destination sees the source as tag:ingress and the tailnet ACL (which MUST allow tag:ingress -> tag:apps:8080/:22 for ingress) lets it through
object=PROVEN 2026-08-07 by apphostd's own log: a bypass connection to the control interface :8092 was logged as "refused 100.70.216.20: grant is held by dash" — 100.70.216.20 is the Mac's tailnet IP (Self tag:ingress). So every OrbStack machine, INCLUDING one logged out of tailscale (no tailscale0 at all), reaches every app's :8080 and :22 by addressing the tailnet IP; the reach is not limited to app envs. A JOINED machine is only INCIDENTALLY blocked because tailscale's own client nft rule drops the relayed reply (ts-input: ip saddr 100.64.0.0/10 iifname != tailscale0 drop — observed 176 pkts dropped on hello); root in the machine removes that or runs `tailscale logout`, so the bypass is available to every env, always. Host pf CANNOT filter it: net.inet.ip.forwarding=0 changed nothing (userspace re-origination, not kernel forwarding), and the relay's egress on utun9 is byte-indistinguishable from legitimate cloudflared (both are 100.70.216.20 -> app 100.x). OrbStack 2.2.1 has NO config to suppress routing 100.64/10 from machines (isolate_network is broken/inverted — blocks the host model service, leaves neighbours reachable). The control plane survived ONLY because apphostd has a SECOND per-grant-address check (client_address in granted_addrs) that the apps' single-layer ACL lacks — and no app-side per-address check can help either, because an app's legitimate ingress client IS the Mac (tag:ingress), the same identity the relay borrows. Root cause: the Mac is simultaneously tag:ingress (ACL must let it reach every app) AND the NAT relay for the machine network onto the tailnet.
